title: Adult size results from both the rate and the duration of growth

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Adult size results from both the rate and the duration of growth

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The size an animal finally attains results from both its rate and its duration of growth: some species are larger because they grow faster (rabbit versus guinea-pig), others because they grow for longer (man versus rabbit).

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. III: The Rate of Growth

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: The size ultimately attained is a resultant of the rate, and of the duration, of growth. It is in the main true, as Minot has said, that the rabbit is bigger than the guinea-pig because he grows the faster; but that man is bigger than the rabbit because he goes on growing for a longer time.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter III, “The Rate of Growth”; topic “Growth curves in other animals”. Scope: animals, especially mammals

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch03-11: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.72

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The decomposition is measurable and can be tested for mammals using public life-history data plus published trajectories. The broad animal scope and lack of standardized curve parameters across species make the full claim only partially resolvable.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Decompose adult size across species into fitted growth rate and duration parameters, then test whether both independently explain final size and whether rabbit–guinea-pig and human–rabbit contrasts follow the stated components. Failure of either component to predict size would refute that part.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Growth rate and duration estimates are statistically correlated.

Phylogeny and ecology confound three-species comparisons.

Databases contain endpoints more often than complete growth trajectories.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.7
operationalizability: 0.9
data adequacy: 0.55
analysis feasibility: 0.7
discriminating power: 0.75

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Rate and duration are separable on existing growth curves, and the three named species are represented in public life-history compilations and human growth standards. That is enough to check the rabbit-guinea pig and human-rabbit contrasts. Extending the result to mammals in general is limited by uneven raw curves, and model-based parameters partly build in the decomposition they are asked to test, so the general claim is only partly resolved.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Decompose adult size into a rate parameter and a duration for human, rabbit, and guinea pig, and then across mammals more generally. The named contrasts predict a higher rate for the rabbit than the guinea pig and a longer duration for the human than the rabbit. A model that uses only rate or only duration should fail if both factors matter.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Nutrition in the classical laboratory comparisons is not standardized across species.

Energy-budget parameters already impose a rate-duration decomposition, so they are not a fully independent test.
